Larger judges show a stronger negative correlation between reward and relative error (bottom right), providing further evidence that capable judges can recover task-relevant structure from reference answers without access to the verifier. Judge accuracy remains above chance throughout training. This may partly reflect differences between generated and reference solutions, since Countdown admits multiple correct answers, though further training may narrow this gap. Even so, the judge’s reward remains informative, guiding the generator toward more accurate solutions. SMILES-to-formula. In this setting, we test RAL on a chemistry task that requires recovering molecular composition from a structured chemical representation. As in the preceding tasks, RAL improves accuracy and learns rewards that track task-relevant errors without access to the evaluator (Figure 4 ). Here, the distinctive result is that RAL, particularly with the 32B judge, improves accuracy faster than training with binary verifiable rewards (top left). One possible explanation is that binary rewards yield zero advantage whenever a prompt’s rollouts are all incorrect or all correct, whereas the judge can assign different scores to these answers and provide a learning signal. We observe nonzero reward advantages on substantially more rollout groups under RAL. This feedback may be particularly useful here because the generator starts at lower accuracy than on the preceding tasks, making groups with no correct answers more common. The reference abstracts come exclusively from biomedical papers, but the generator does not receive explicit domain instructions. Because a frozen judge (with sufficient prompting) can in theory determine the domain and quality of an abstract, we compare RAL against rewards from a frozen judge (Claude Haiku 4.5 Anthropic (2025) ). To make the discrimination task easier for Haiku, we present a generated abstract alongside a randomly sampled real reference abstract and ask it to identify the real one. The generator receives a binary reward of 1.0 1.0 if Haiku selects the generated abstract as real, and 0.0 0.0 otherwise. We also explicitly tell Haiku the target domain by including the following sentence in its prompt: “The real paper corpus contains medical and biomedical paper abstracts.” Thus, the frozen judge receives both a reference abstract for direct comparison and explicit domain information. The frozen-judge prompt is provided in Appendix D . We evaluate whether generated abstracts match the target topic distribution and how semantically diverse they are. Domain alignment is measured as the fraction of abstracts classified as clearly biomedical by Claude Haiku 4.5 using a separate evaluation prompt (Appendix D ). Semantic diversity is computed as the mean pairwise cosine distance between embeddings computed with OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model ( OpenAI, 2024 ) . Figure 5 shows that optimization against the frozen judge steadily increases reward (left) while reducing semantic diversity (middle) and failing to recover the biomedical domain (right). At the final checkpoint, 125 of 128 generations collapse onto a Pacific-oyster microplastics ecotoxicology theme despite remaining lexically distinct (Appendix D.3 ). RAL instead drives the biomedical rate toward one while preserving diversity. Diversity initially falls, then recovers to approximately its starting level while domain fidelity remains high. These results show that RAL can recover the target domain from reference examples alone without collapsing onto a narrow topic. During training, RAL generator reward and judge accuracy show a sawtooth pattern as the generator and judge adapt to each other. This pattern is consistent with the generator learning features that fool the current judge, raising reward, followed by the judge learning to distinguish the new generations, lowering reward and redirecting learning toward remaining differences from the references. Alongside these judge dynamics, qualitative inspection suggests that the generated abstracts develop more coherent scientific arguments. Later outputs include hypotheses motivated by purported preliminary findings, aims designed to test those hypotheses, and experiments that address alternative explanations. Qualitative inspection also suggests that reasoning traces become more specific and more closely reflected in the final abstracts. Early traces are generic and tentative, while later traces reason from those findings to hypotheses, consider alternative explanations, and weigh the scope and limits of the proposed work. These changes occur even though the judge never sees the traces and they receive no direct supervision. These observations suggest that co-training helps the generator to progressively capture the underlying structure of reference abstracts, including how they connect problems, mechanisms, and proposed experiments. Our qualitative analysis covers only a subset of generations and does not capture the full range of patterns learned during training, particularly subtler distinctions. LLM judges may detect subtle differences between generated and reference abstracts that human evaluators miss, potentially explaining their lower fooling rates, though we do not test this explanation directly. 5 Limitations and future work Our study has several limitations. To isolate judge capacity and co-training duration, we keep most other hyperparameters fixed across settings and do not perform extensive task-specific sweeps. Task (and judge size) specific tuning may improve both convergence and final performance. On the NIH grant experiment, RAL faces stability challenges associated with adversarial co-training. Despite the fluctuations in fooling rate seen in Figure 6 (left), RAL repeatedly recovers from performance drops and reaches fooling rates above the frontier-model baselines at multiple checkpoints, leaving room to improve stability while preserving these gains. Furthermore, the generator is not currently conditioned on specific research results, only on the title. Conditioning it on real results and providing those results to the judge is a natural next step. Judge capacity is another practical bottleneck. Larger judges consistently learn better rewards, and some tasks require judges substantially larger than the generator to match verifiable-reward training. This increases training cost, though the judge can be discarded at inference time. Better judge initialization, specialized pretraining, or more efficient judge architectures may reduce this requirement. Continued improvements in model capability and inference efficiency may also make large judges increasingly practical, easing this bottleneck. 6 Conclusion Our work shows that reference final answers alone can support effective RL post-training of reasoning models. RAL uses a simple supervised judge, trained alongside the generator but scaled independently, to turn reference data into an adaptive training objective. The judge’s predicted reference probability serves as the sole reward, without verifiers, reward labels, or expert reasoning traces. Useful reasoning is therefore learned through outcome-level feedback. On tasks with hidden verifiable rewards, this learned signal can match or exceed direct reward optimization. On open-ended scientific generation, RAL recovers a target domain from reference examples without explicit domain instructions, while preserving diversity. On NIH grant generation, it surpasses strong frontier-LLM baselines in fooling both LLM judges and human experts. Across settings, judge capacity and sufficient co-training are key to making this simple reward signal effective. These results suggest that modern LLM judges can recover task-relevant structure from reference answers and support the view that adversarial co-training can provide a curriculum that moves beyond superficial cues. The results across arithmetic, code, chemistry, and scientific writing motivate further study of this approach in scientific and other high-value domains where good answers are easier to collect than to score. We use 5,000 biomedical and medical abstracts drawn from an enriched corpus of scientific paper abstracts. To construct the corpus, we queried Google Scholar using keywords across biology and medicine. We used a language model to extract each paper’s title and abstract, excluding running headers, keywords, affiliations, and body sections. We then matched papers to OpenAlex by title to verify their domain and record their field, publication date, and citation count. We retained papers classified by OpenAlex as medical or biomedical whose abstracts were well formed, contained 200–350 words, and did not exceed 3,000 characters. We removed duplicates based on normalized abstract text, shuffled the remaining abstracts with a fixed seed, and selected the first 5,000. Almost all selected papers were published between 2024 and 2026, with a median publication year of 2025. These abstracts define the real data distribution that the generator learns to imitate in our adversarial experiments. Each example consists of a real paper abstract. The generator receives no paper title and is prompted only to produce a scientifically plausible research paper abstract.
